{"label": "Accuser Statement Audio", "title": "Lauren Deal — Police Interview Audio Archive", "strength": "Strength: Corroborated", "tags": ["Accuser Statement", "Contradiction", "Audio", "Impeachment", "Narrative Engineering"], "discussion": "Interview with Officer Haines: Lauren Deal: So he takes me inside but he doesn't take me to like a normal bathroom and he takes me to the bathroom in his bedroom and I told him to get out because I had to pee and he stood in the doorway and he told me that he was going to watch me. So I still pulled my pants down because I had to pee and I was like just please get out.

Interview with Detective Freeman: Lauren Deal: "It was it was no later than 245, so I walked inside, and I've been in this house before because I've been in there with Tiffany. So I knew where everything was, and he told me to use the restroom in his room. So like, when you walk into his room, it's his room, and then his bathroom is back there. So I walked back there, and he followed me into the bathroom and stood in the doorway, and I was like, you know, I said get out. I have to pee, he's like, no, I'm gonna stand here. Detective Freeman: So why did he say that he was gonna stand here? Lauren Deal: "I don't know. He's never; he's never made advances like that before. So. I don't know. I mean, I still sat down to pee because I had to pee. And I kept telling him to turn around and not look at me. And then, when I was done, I got up I pull my pants up to flush the toilet. I went to walk out of the bathroom, and when I did, I got grabbed and pushed backwards onto his bed."

Court Testimony Direct by Prosecution LAUREN DEAL: It's like the air changed in there. And I still had to pee, so I went into the bathroom, and he stood in the doorway, and I told him I did not want him to watch me pee, to please turn around." MS. BARTHOLOMEW: "Did the defendant turn around?" LAUREN DEAL: shakes head. "No."

Cross Examination by Defense MR. WUNSCH: Now, your testimony is that you state that Ben stood in the doorframe while you were using the restroom, correct? The bathroom, correct? I would say restroom, but bathroom, correct? And then you said that you urinated, correct? LAUREN DEAL: I did. MR. WUNSCH: Now, in the opening, the prosecution stated that you asked him to turn around and he did, is that correct? He turned around while you were urinating and didn't watch you? LAUREN DEAL: He stood in the doorframe. MR. WUNSCH: But turned around while -- he was not, like, in the opening. It was stated to the jury that while you were urinating, he turned -- you asked him to turn around, and so he turned around, is that correct? LAUREN DEAL: Halfway. MR. WUNSCH: Is that correct? LAUREN DEAL: Halfway. MR. WUNSCH: Halfway turned around? So as not to watch you urinating, correct? LAUREN DEAL: Halfway. MR. WUNSCH: Okay. What does "halfway" mean? LAUREN DEAL: Literally halfway. He was not fully turned around but he was not completely facing me. He was halfway turned. MR. WUNSCH: Okay. So it's a halfway turn. And you never stated anything about that to police after that happened, correct? That he turned around halfway while you're urinating? LAUREN DEAL: I told police exactly what happened. MR. WUNSCH: Okay. So you say he halfway turned around while you were urinating. And at that time, was he making any sexual remarks to you? LAUREN DEAL: No, he was just standing there.

The key point is that a fabricated event has no fixed episodic memory anchoring it. The speaker must repeatedly reconstruct the account from the story already told, the questions being asked, and the evidentiary needs of the moment. That can produce exactly the kind of drift seen in these multiple statements.

The significance of these inconsistencies depends on whether the event actually occurred. If Deal was recounting a genuine event, differences in wording might reasonably be attributed to ordinary memory variation, interviewer emphasis, or later elaboration. The defense contends that the episode was fabricated, and the changing versions are relevant because they are more consistent with reconstruction of an invented account than with recall of a fixed historical event. On that premise, there was no underlying event for Deal to remember. What had to remain consistent was not a memory, but a narrative. The record shows that narrative changing in ways that affect its meaning: Allen first “takes” her to the bathroom, later merely tells her which bathroom to use, and at trial she simply says she went there; he first says he is going to “watch” her, later says only that he will “stand here,” and at trial she acknowledges that he made no sexual remarks; she initially describes telling him to get out, later emphasizes asking him to turn around; and at trial she first says he did not turn around before conceding on cross-examination that he turned “halfway.” These are not merely differences in vocabulary. They alter the conduct from which the State asks the jury to infer control, sexual intent, and escalating menace. If the event was invented, the changing details are consistent with a story being reconstructed rather than an actual event being recalled.

The story changed at the pressure points where the narrative derives its incriminating meaning.

The credibility problem is sharpened by testimony from the State's own witness, Steve Happel. According to Happel, he overheard ADA Tiffany Bartholomew tell Lauren Deal that she “should have said she was afraid of the witnesses.”

The wording matters. This was not, as reported, a neutral question asking Deal what she remembered or how she felt. Happel described the prosecutor telling Deal what she “should have said.” And the suggested subject was not incidental. Fear supplied an explanation capable of reconciling conduct that might otherwise appear inconsistent with the State's portrayal of the events.

That evidence must be considered alongside the evolution of Deal's account. Her early descriptions focused primarily upon physical events and specific statements. By trial, subjective fear and atmospheric language had assumed greater prominence. The bathroom encounter, for example, acquired the characterization that “the air changed.” Elsewhere, fear became an increasingly important explanation for behavior that otherwise required explanation.

Standing alone, changes in emotional language might be attributed to ordinary differences in retelling. Happel's testimony creates a materially different issue. If a prosecutor was heard telling Deal that she “should have said she was afraid,” then later fear-based explanations cannot simply be assumed to represent spontaneous recollection without examining when those explanations first appeared.

The relevant chronology therefore becomes critical: what Deal said before the conversation Happel overheard; exactly what Bartholomew told her; what Deal said afterward; and whether the suggested explanation appeared only after the prosecutor supplied it. If the record shows that Deal had not previously claimed fear of the witnesses and later adopted that explanation, the sequence supports an inference of testimonial shaping rather than independent recollection.

The point is not that legitimate witness preparation is prohibited. Attorneys may review evidence and prepare witnesses to testify truthfully. The distinction is between helping a witness communicate an independently held memory and supplying an explanation that the witness had not previously given. Happel's account, if credited, places that distinction directly at issue because the prosecutor allegedly did not ask Deal whether she had been afraid of the witnesses; she told Deal that she “should have said” that she was."}
